title: The capital stack: who is paid first and who loses first
summary: Every development is funded by layers of money that rank in a fixed order: senior debt, then subordinated debt, then preferred equity, then common equity. The senior bank is paid first and loses last, and it sizes its loan by how thick the cushion below it is.
body:
The capital stack is the ranking of everyone who funded a project, from the senior lender who is paid first to the common equity that is paid last. Mr Shabazz, the bank sits at the top, and everything below it, including your money, is its cushion.

In plain English

Picture the money in a project as a stack of layers. When cash comes in, from rent or from a sale, it is paid to the top layer first until that layer is satisfied, then to the next, and so on down. When things go wrong, losses are absorbed from the bottom up. The bottom layer loses everything before the layer above it loses anything.

That ordering explains the price of each layer. The top layer takes the least risk, so it accepts the lowest return. The bottom layer takes the first loss, so it expects all the upside.

The professional framing: the four layers

Senior secured debt

Paid first, from all cash flow and from any sale, and secured by a first-ranking mortgage. Lowest cost to you. This is the bank.

Mezzanine or subordinated debt

A loan that ranks after the senior loan. It is paid only once senior debt service is met, and on a sale only after the senior loan is repaid in full. Because it takes more risk, it costs more. A senior bank accepts mezzanine debt only if it is fully subordinated and cannot enforce its own rights without the senior lender's consent.

Preferred equity

Equity that receives a fixed priority return before common equity, but after all debt. A senior bank will usually treat it as equity, part of its cushion, only if it has no right to be repaid before the bank and no security over the property.

Common equity

You, your partners and your land contribution. Paid last, takes the first loss, and owns everything left after all the layers above are satisfied. This is the layer that makes or loses fortunes.

The professional framing: the cushion and the price

A senior lender's question is: how much can the value fall before my loan is impaired? The answer is the thickness of everything below it. If the senior loan is 65 percent of value, the cushion is 35 percent. Adding mezzanine debt does not thicken the senior lender's cushion in any way that matters to the sponsor, because it is still debt that must be serviced; it does let the sponsor put in less common equity, at a higher cost and with higher risk of losing that equity.

A worked example

A hypothetical project cost US$1,000,000, funded as follows: senior loan US$650,000, mezzanine loan US$150,000, preferred equity US$100,000, common equity US$100,000. The project fails, and the building is sold for US$900,000, with US$50,000 of sale and enforcement costs, leaving US$850,000 to distribute. Ignore accrued interest for simplicity.

  1. Senior debt is paid US$650,000 in full. Remaining: US$200,000.
  2. Mezzanine is paid US$150,000 in full. Remaining: US$50,000.
  3. Preferred equity receives US$50,000 of its US$100,000, a 50 percent loss.
  4. Common equity receives nothing, a 100 percent loss.

A 15 percent fall in value against cost, plus costs of sale, wiped out the bottom layer entirely and half of the next. The senior lender was untouched. Now run the upside: if the building sells for US$1,400,000, the debt and the preferred return are paid fixed amounts and common equity keeps all of the surplus. That asymmetry is why common equity is the most expensive money you will ever raise, and the most valuable money you will ever own.

The professional framing: cash flow versus sale

The stack applies twice. In operation, monthly rent is paid out in order: operating costs, senior debt service, mezzanine interest, the preferred return, and only then distributions to common equity. On a sale or refinance, the proceeds follow the same order. The documents that set this order for the cash are called the waterfall. A sponsor who forgets that common equity sits at the bottom of the operating waterfall is surprised to find no distributions while a building is still leasing up.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is over-layering. Each layer above common equity is a fixed claim that must be paid regardless of how the building performs. A stack with senior debt, mezzanine and a preferred return can leave so little cash for common equity that a modest rent shortfall stops all distributions, and a modest fall in value erases the equity entirely. More layers mean more leverage, and leverage cuts both ways.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats mezzanine or preferred money as "more equity" because it is not from the bank. To you it may feel like equity; to the senior lender, any layer with a fixed return, a repayment date or security is debt-like, and it may be counted as debt in the credit memo. Next lesson covers exactly which features change the classification.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, draw your project's stack as a simple column with each layer's amount, cost and ranking. Then run the waterfall twice: once on a sale at 15 percent below cost and once at 30 percent above. Read off what each layer receives. If you would not accept your own common-equity outcome in the downside case, the stack is too thin at the bottom. Professional sign-off required: lawyer for intercreditor and waterfall terms, and a securities or corporate lawyer before raising any investor money, because offering equity to investors is regulated in most jurisdictions.
checklist: Senior secured debt is paid first and loses last.
Mezzanine ranks after senior debt and costs more; the senior bank requires it to be fully subordinated.
Preferred equity gets a priority return after debt and before common equity.
Common equity is paid last, takes the first loss and keeps all the upside.
The same order applies to monthly cash (the waterfall) and to sale proceeds.
More layers mean more fixed claims and more leverage.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A project's stack is senior US$600,000, mezzanine US$200,000 and common equity US$200,000. It sells for US$700,000 net of costs. What does each layer receive?
selftest.a: Senior receives US$600,000 in full. Mezzanine receives the remaining US$100,000, a 50 percent loss. Common equity receives nothing, a total loss. A 30 percent fall against total cost wiped out the equity and half the mezzanine while the senior lender was repaid in full.

apply: Draw a four-layer capital stack for a hypothetical US$2,000,000 project and run the sale waterfall at 15 percent below cost.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Parts 6 and 7. The capital stack and what lenders count as equity are commercial practice. Security instruments, guarantees, enforcement and priority are matters of law that differ between countries and states; everything here is a concept only [unverified — confirm with a lawyer in the jurisdiction where the land and the borrower sit].

title: What a bank counts as equity, and the intercreditor agreement
summary: A bank counts money as equity only if it is paid in, cannot be repaid or secured ahead of the bank, and carries no hidden guarantees. Where there is more than one lender, an intercreditor agreement sets who is paid when and who may enforce.
body:
Money only counts as equity to a bank if it is actually paid in, ranks behind the bank, and carries no side deal that turns it into debt. Mr Shabazz, investor terms you agree casually can quietly shrink your loan, so read every investor term through the bank's eyes before you sign it.

In plain English

You may think of all non-bank money as equity. The bank does not. It asks a simple question of every dollar below it: if this project gets into trouble, will this money stand behind us, or will it compete with us for the cash? Money that stands behind the bank is equity. Money that competes with it, however it is labelled, is treated as debt.

The professional framing: four rules for what counts

  1. Paid in, not promised. The evidence is bank statements, escrow confirmations or invoices already paid. A signed commitment from an investor who has not yet transferred money is not equity yet.
  2. Cannot be repaid, redeemed or secured ahead of the bank. If the investor can demand its money back before the bank's loan is repaid, or holds security over the property, it ranks with or ahead of the bank in practice.
  3. No side letters, guarantees or demand notes. A private promise that the sponsor will personally repay an investor, or a guaranteed minimum return paid regardless of performance, makes that money debt-like.
  4. Land counts at a value the bank accepts. Usually its own appraisal, sometimes the lower of what you paid and what it is worth [unverified — lender-specific].

The professional framing: what lenders discount or exclude

  • Contractor deferrals. A contractor agreeing to defer part of its fee until completion is a creditor, not an equity holder, and may have lien rights.
  • Verbal investor commitments. Not paid in, so not counted.
  • Future pre-sale deposits. Money that may be refundable to buyers, and may be legally restricted, is usually excluded or discounted.
  • Your own development fee. Paying yourself a fee and calling the unpaid part equity is usually rejected, or credited only in part.

The professional framing: the intercreditor agreement

Where there is more than one lender, the senior lender will insist on a signed intercreditor agreement. It sets the order of payment, which lender may enforce and when, what the junior lender may do on default, whether the junior lender can buy out the senior loan, and standstill periods during which the junior lender must wait before acting. Without one, a senior bank will rarely allow any other debt on the project at all.

The professional framing: when equity must be spent

Counting is one question; timing is another. Most construction lenders require all counted equity to be spent before the first loan draw, so the bank's money is never at risk while yours is still sitting in an account. Some will accept equity spent in proportion with the loan, called pro rata funding, or will accept an irrevocable letter of credit or cash held in a blocked account in place of equity spent upfront [unverified — lender-specific]. Pro rata funding lowers your interest cost and your early exposure, so it is worth asking for. In exchange, expect the bank to want stronger evidence that the remaining equity is genuinely available, such as funds held in escrow under its control.

A worked example

A hypothetical project costs US$1,000,000. The bank lends at 65 percent of cost and requires US$350,000 of equity. The sponsor presents the following.

  1. US$150,000 of cash already spent on design and approvals. Counted in full.
  2. Land bought for US$100,000 and appraised at US$140,000. This bank credits land at the lower of cost and value: US$100,000.
  3. US$80,000 from an investor promising to transfer next month. Not counted until paid in.
  4. US$50,000 from a second investor who is guaranteed a 12 percent return and repayment in two years, before the loan matures. Treated as debt.
  5. US$40,000 of contractor fee deferred to completion. Excluded.

Total presented: US$420,000. Total the bank counts: US$150,000 plus US$100,000, which is US$250,000, US$100,000 short of the requirement. The sponsor must either bring in the first investor's cash now, restructure the second investor's terms so repayment falls after the bank and carries no guarantee, or reduce the loan. Worse, the second investor's terms may now count as debt in the coverage test, reducing the loan further.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is discovering the classification problem at credit committee. A preferred return with a fixed redemption date before loan maturity can turn your equity into debt in the credit memo, shrinking the loan and raising the debt service, weeks after you have signed with the investor. Unwinding an investor agreement is slow and damages relationships.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts everything that is not the bank's money as equity, and presents a total that the bank then cuts. Present only what the bank will count, and list separately anything committed but not yet paid in. A committee that sees you have already applied its own rules trusts the rest of the file more.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, before agreeing any investor term, send a one-paragraph summary to your relationship manager and ask how it would be treated in the credit memo. Prepare an equity schedule with three columns: paid in with evidence, committed but not paid, and excluded or doubtful, and total only the first. Ask each lender how it credits land and whether it accepts equity spent pro rata with the loan. Professional sign-off required: lawyer for investor agreements and any intercreditor agreement; securities lawyer before any investor offering.

The same habit protects you with investors as well. If you tell an investor clearly, before they commit, that their money must rank behind the bank and cannot be repaid before the loan, you avoid the far harder conversation of renegotiating after the bank has objected.
checklist: Equity must be paid in, with evidence, not promised.
Money that can be repaid, redeemed or secured ahead of the bank is treated as debt.
Side letters, guarantees and fixed redemption dates turn equity into debt.
Land is credited at a value the lender accepts, often its own appraisal or the lower of cost and value.
Contractor deferrals, verbal commitments and refundable deposits are usually excluded.
Multiple lenders need a signed intercreditor agreement setting priority and enforcement.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: An investor offers US$200,000 as 'preferred equity' with a 10 percent fixed return and a right to be repaid in 18 months; your bank loan has a three-year term. How will the bank likely treat it, and what would you change?
selftest.a: Because it must be repaid before the bank loan matures, with a fixed return, the bank will likely treat it as debt: it will not count toward the equity requirement and may enter the coverage test. Change the terms so repayment can occur only after the senior loan is repaid or refinanced, with no security and no personal guarantee, and confirm the treatment with the bank before signing.

apply: Prepare a three-column equity schedule for a hypothetical project: paid in with evidence, committed but not paid, excluded or doubtful.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Parts 6 and 7. The capital stack and what lenders count as equity are commercial practice. Security instruments, guarantees, enforcement and priority are matters of law that differ between countries and states; everything here is a concept only [unverified — confirm with a lawyer in the jurisdiction where the land and the borrower sit].

title: The security package: what the bank can take
summary: Security is the set of legal rights that let a bank take and sell assets if the loan fails. A development lender typically asks for a first mortgage, a charge over the borrower's assets, assignments of leases, insurance and contracts, a pledge of the borrower's shares and control of key accounts.
body:
Security is the bank's second way out: the legal right to take and sell specific assets if the loan is not repaid. Mr Shabazz, a development lender takes security not only over the building but over its rents, its insurance, its contracts and the company that owns it, so it can either sell the asset or step in and finish it.

In plain English

When you take a mortgage on a house, the bank can sell the house if you stop paying. A development loan works on the same idea, but the bank wants more, because a half-built or partly leased building is not easy to sell. It wants to be able to collect the rent, receive any insurance payout, take over the construction contract to finish the work, and if necessary take over the company itself. Each of these needs its own legal document, and together they are called the security package.

The professional framing: the typical package

The names and mechanics differ by country and state, so treat this as a map of concepts, not a legal checklist [unverified — confirm each instrument with a lawyer in the jurisdiction].

  • First registered mortgage over the land and building. The right to sell the property on default, ranking ahead of any later claim. In some places the instrument is called a deed of trust or a charge.
  • A charge over the borrower's other assets. In many Commonwealth jurisdictions this is a debenture with fixed and floating charges; in the United States the comparable concept is a security interest over personal property, perfected by a public filing. It covers accounts, equipment and other company assets.
  • Assignment of leases and rents. If you default, rents are paid to the bank.
  • Assignment of insurance. The bank is named as loss payee, so a fire or flood payout goes to the bank first.
  • Assignment of the construction contract and warranties. Often with a direct agreement signed by the contractor, so the bank can step in and finish the building rather than sell a shell.
  • Share pledge over the borrowing company. The bank can take control of the company, not only the asset, which can be faster and cheaper than enforcing a mortgage.
  • Account control. Rent accounts and a debt service reserve held at the bank, where it can see and, on default, control the cash.

The professional framing: registration and priority

Security over land is registered in the place where the land sits, under that place's law; the location of the bank or the borrower does not change that. A mortgage that is signed but not registered may not rank ahead of a later claim. Priority is generally set by the order of registration, subject to exceptions such as certain tax claims and, in some places, construction liens [unverified — confirm locally]. This is why lenders insist on registration before the first draw, and why title searches are repeated at each draw in some markets.

A worked example

A hypothetical borrower has a US$650,000 loan on a building that is 80 percent complete when the borrower becomes insolvent. Consider the bank's options with and without the full package.

  1. Mortgage only. The bank enforces and sells an unfinished building. Buyers discount for unknown work and the cost of restarting. It sells for perhaps US$500,000 after costs, a US$150,000 loss.
  2. Full package. The bank uses its assignment of the construction contract to keep the contractor working, funds the last 20 percent of cost, say US$150,000, and uses its share pledge to take control of the borrowing company without a lengthy court sale. On completion the building is worth US$1,000,000. The bank recovers its US$650,000 plus the US$150,000 it advanced, with room to spare.

The difference between those outcomes is the step-in rights. That is why lenders insist on documents that look excessive to a borrower who has never needed them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk, for the bank and therefore for you, is security that cannot be registered or enforced: land not yet in the borrower's name, a title defect, an unregistered easement, or a security document governed by the wrong law. If a lender's lawyer cannot give a clean opinion that the security is valid and enforceable, there is no loan, however strong the project.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leaves title and entity work until after the commitment letter. Land held personally, a borrowing company not yet formed, or an undecided structure such as whether land is contributed or ground-leased will each stop the security package. These take weeks or months and cost legal fees; start them early, because they are almost always conditions precedent.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, ask each lender for its standard security list at the appetite stage, not at documentation. Commission a title search early, resolve every defect, and transfer the land into the borrowing company if that is the structure. Brief your contractor that a direct agreement with the bank will be required, so it is priced and accepted in the construction contract. Keep insurance policies ready to name the lender as loss payee. Professional sign-off required: real estate and banking lawyer in the jurisdiction where the land sits, who will also issue or review the legal opinion the lender requires.

From your operations background, think of the security package as the lender's isolation and recovery procedure. It is written before anything fails, it is tested on paper, and its value is entirely in how quickly it lets someone take control when the normal system stops working.
checklist: A first registered mortgage gives the right to sell the property on default.
A charge or security interest covers the borrower's other assets, such as accounts and equipment.
Assignments of rents, insurance and the construction contract let the bank collect income, claim payouts and step in.
A share pledge lets the bank take control of the borrowing company.
Security over land is registered where the land sits, under that place's law.
Fix title and form the borrowing company before you apply; both are usually conditions precedent.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your lender's lawyer cannot issue a clean opinion because the land is still in your personal name and the borrowing company has not been formed. Why does this stop the loan, and what must happen?
selftest.a: Without the land owned by the borrower and a validly formed borrower, the bank cannot take an enforceable first mortgage or the other security, so it has no second way out and its lawyer cannot confirm enforceability. The company must be formed, authorised to borrow, and the land transferred to it (or the chosen structure documented), with title cleared and security registered before the first draw. Take tax and legal advice on the transfer.

apply: Write the seven items of a typical development security package and, beside each, the document or step you would need to deliver it.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Parts 6 and 7. The capital stack and what lenders count as equity are commercial practice. Security instruments, guarantees, enforcement and priority are matters of law that differ between countries and states; everything here is a concept only [unverified — confirm with a lawyer in the jurisdiction where the land and the borrower sit].

title: Guarantees, covenants and events of default
summary: Guarantees decide who else must pay if the project cannot; covenants are the promises that let a bank act before things get worse; events of default are the breaches that let it stop lending and enforce. The guarantee is the most consequential document a sponsor signs.
body:
A guarantee makes you personally liable for some or all of the loan; covenants are the tripwires; events of default are what happens when one is tripped. Mr Shabazz, never sign a guarantee as a formality, because it is the document that turns a project failure into a personal one.

In plain English

A development loan is usually made to a company that owns only the project. If the project fails, the company has nothing else. So the bank asks a person with assets, the sponsor, to promise to pay in certain situations. That promise is a guarantee. The bank also writes rules into the loan that it can check every month or quarter, so it can see trouble coming. Those rules are covenants. A breach of a covenant, or a missed payment, is an event of default, which gives the bank the right to act.

The professional framing: types of guarantee

  • Full-recourse personal guarantee. You personally repay any shortfall on the loan, whatever the cause. Your other assets, possibly in other countries, become reachable through enforcement of a court judgment [unverified — cross-border enforcement is a legal question for counsel].
  • Completion guarantee. You guarantee that the building will be finished, on time and to specification, then the guarantee falls away.
  • Cost-overrun guarantee. You fund any cost above the budget.
  • Interest and carry guarantee. You cover interest and operating shortfalls until the building is stabilised.
  • Limited guarantees. Capped at a fixed amount or percentage of the loan, or triggered only by specific bad acts such as fraud or unauthorised transfer, sometimes called carve-outs.

The negotiating goal for a first-time sponsor is limited guarantees that burn off at completion or stabilisation, and never an open-ended full-recourse guarantee if it can be avoided.

The professional framing: covenants

  • Financial covenants. A minimum coverage ratio, a maximum loan-to-value, and a minimum sponsor liquidity or net worth.
  • Reporting covenants. Monthly draw reports during construction, quarterly accounts, annual audited or reviewed statements, rent rolls and insurance certificates.
  • Negative covenants. No further debt, no change of control, no sale or further charge of the property, and no distributions to equity while any covenant is in breach.

The professional framing: events of default and cure

Typical events of default include a missed payment, a covenant breach, a false representation, insolvency, a change of control, an unfunded cost overrun and a missed completion date. Default usually lets the bank stop further draws, demand repayment of the whole loan, and enforce its security. Loan documents normally give a cure period for some defaults, for example a number of days to make a late payment or to fund a coverage shortfall with cash. Negotiating cure rights before signing is far easier than after.

The professional framing: what the guarantor's covenants require

A guarantee usually comes with covenants on the guarantor as well as on the borrower. A common one is a minimum liquidity or net worth test: the guarantor promises to hold, say, a stated amount of unencumbered cash and securities throughout the loan, and to provide personal financial statements each year. Breaching it is an event of default on the loan, even if the building is performing perfectly. These tests can restrict what you do with your own money, such as buying another property or paying down a personal mortgage, so read them with your wider plans in mind. Lenders also commonly ask for notice before the guarantor takes on other guarantees, because each new one competes for the same assets.

A worked example

A hypothetical sponsor guarantees a US$650,000 construction loan. The project fails and the bank sells the building.

  1. Net sale proceeds after enforcement costs: US$500,000. Shortfall on principal: US$150,000.
  2. Accrued default interest and the bank's legal costs: US$30,000. Total shortfall: US$180,000.
  3. Under a full-recourse guarantee, the sponsor owes US$180,000 personally.
  4. Under a guarantee capped at 20 percent of the loan, the sponsor owes at most US$130,000.
  5. Under a completion guarantee that burned off when the building was finished, and a failure that happened afterwards during lease-up, the sponsor may owe nothing under the guarantee, though the equity is still lost.

The same failure costs the sponsor US$180,000, US$130,000 or nothing, decided entirely by wording signed months earlier.

Notice also that default interest and enforcement costs, which a full-recourse guarantee usually covers, grow every month the recovery takes. A slow enforcement in a busy court system can add materially to the shortfall, which is one more reason a bank prefers fast remedies such as a share pledge, and one more reason a guarantor wants a cap.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the interaction between a guarantee and your other assets. A full-recourse guarantee moves the project's risk onto your personal balance sheet, including your home, savings and other businesses, and possibly assets held jointly with family. That is a wealth-planning decision, not only a financing one, and it deserves advice from someone who represents only you.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner signs the bank's standard guarantee because "everyone signs it" and the loan is otherwise agreed. Guarantee terms are often negotiable, especially the cap, the burn-off trigger and the carve-outs, but only before signing. Also read the definitions: a guarantee of "all obligations" may cover far more than the loan amount, including costs, interest and swap obligations.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, list every guarantee a lender proposes with three facts each: what it covers, its maximum amount, and the exact event that ends it. Then write the worst-case figure for each beside your liquid assets. Ask for completion and overrun guarantees that burn off at completion, and carry guarantees that burn off at stabilisation, instead of full recourse. Diarise every covenant test date, and model each financial covenant monthly so a breach is foreseen, not discovered. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer acting only for you on every guarantee, and on cross-border enforcement if your assets are in a different country from the project.
checklist: Full recourse makes you personally liable for any shortfall.
Completion, overrun and carry guarantees should burn off at completion or stabilisation.
Financial, reporting and negative covenants let the bank act early.
Events of default let the bank stop draws, demand repayment and enforce security.
Negotiate caps, burn-off triggers and cure periods before signing.
A guarantee is a personal wealth decision; take independent legal advice.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A bank proposes a full-recourse personal guarantee for the life of a five-year construction-to-term loan. What would you counter-propose, and why?
selftest.a: Counter with a completion guarantee and a cost-overrun guarantee that burn off at practical completion, an interest and carry guarantee that burns off when stabilisation is reached, and carve-out liability only for fraud or unauthorised transfers thereafter, with any remaining recourse capped at a fixed amount. This limits personal exposure to the periods of real risk while still giving the bank the protection it needs during construction and lease-up.

apply: For a hypothetical loan, write each proposed guarantee with what it covers, its maximum amount and the event that ends it.

title: Week 4 review: the capital stack, security and guarantees
summary: Six questions on the capital stack, what counts as equity, intercreditor agreements, security and guarantees. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.
body:
This week was about ranking and remedies: who gets paid first, what counts as your money, what the bank can take, and what you personally promise. Mr Shabazz, answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

Question 1. List the four layers of the capital stack from safest to riskiest and say how each is paid.

Answer. Senior secured debt is paid first from all cash flow and from any sale, at the lowest cost. Mezzanine or subordinated debt is paid after senior debt, at a higher cost, and must be fully subordinated to satisfy the senior bank. Preferred equity receives a fixed priority return after all debt and before common equity. Common equity, meaning you, your partners and your land, is paid last, takes the first loss and keeps all the upside. The same order applies to monthly cash in the waterfall and to sale proceeds.

Question 2. A stack is senior US$650,000, mezzanine US$150,000, preferred US$100,000 and common US$100,000. Net sale proceeds are US$850,000. What does each layer receive?

Answer. Senior receives US$650,000, leaving US$200,000. Mezzanine receives US$150,000, leaving US$50,000. Preferred receives US$50,000 of US$100,000. Common receives nothing. A 15 percent fall in value plus costs of sale wiped out the common equity and half the preferred while the senior lender was untouched.

Question 3. What three features turn money you call equity into debt in a credit memo?

Answer. A right to be repaid or redeemed before the bank, for example a fixed redemption date before the loan matures; security over the property or a claim that ranks with the bank; and a guarantee or side letter, such as a sponsor's personal promise of repayment or a guaranteed return regardless of performance. Money also does not count if it is only promised and not paid in.

Question 4. What does an intercreditor agreement do, and when will a senior bank insist on one?

Answer. It sets the order of payment between lenders, which lender may enforce and when, what the junior lender may do on default, any standstill period and any right of the junior lender to buy out the senior loan. A senior bank insists on one whenever any other lender, such as a mezzanine lender, has a claim on the project, and without one will rarely allow other debt at all.

Question 5. Why does a development lender want an assignment of the construction contract and a share pledge, and not only a mortgage?

Answer. A half-built building sells at a deep discount, so a mortgage alone may leave a large loss. The contract assignment and a direct agreement with the contractor let the bank step in and finish the building, and the share pledge lets it take control of the borrowing company quickly rather than through a long court sale. Together they turn a distressed asset into a finished one worth far more.

Question 6. Distinguish a completion guarantee from a full-recourse personal guarantee.

Answer. A completion guarantee promises that the building will be finished, on time and to specification, and falls away at completion; it covers construction risk only. A full-recourse personal guarantee makes the sponsor personally liable for any shortfall on the whole loan, whatever the cause and for its whole term, reaching the sponsor's other assets. The first is a limited, time-bound commitment; the second moves the entire project risk onto the sponsor's personal balance sheet.

Recap

The capital stack ranks every source of money. Senior debt is paid first and loses last; common equity is paid last and loses first. Each extra layer above common equity is a fixed claim that increases leverage. A bank counts money as equity only when it is paid in, ranks behind the bank and carries no side deal, and land is credited at a value the lender accepts. Multiple lenders need an intercreditor agreement.

The security package gives the bank its second way out: a registered first mortgage, a charge over the borrower's assets, assignments of rents, insurance and the construction contract, a share pledge and account control. Security is registered where the land sits, so title and entity work must be finished early. Guarantees decide what you personally owe; negotiate limited guarantees that burn off at completion or stabilisation. Covenants are tripwires, events of default are the consequences, and cure rights are worth negotiating before you sign.

Mr Shabazz, the most important single habit from this week is to write down, before you sign anything, the worst-case personal cost of every guarantee and compare it with your liquid assets. Next week takes the same tools across borders: comparing lending markets, withholding tax and gross-up, currency mismatch, and decoding a term sheet line by line.

Two calculation habits are worth practising until they are automatic. First, the sale waterfall: given a stack and a net sale price, pay each layer in order and read off who loses what. Second, the guarantee shortfall: net proceeds against principal, plus accrued interest and costs, compared with any cap. Both take under a minute with round numbers, and both answer the question a committee and a guarantor each care about most.

Keep in mind, too, how this week connects with the last. The equity rules decide how thick the cushion below the bank is, the security package decides how much of the asset the bank can recover through that cushion, and the guarantees decide what happens if the cushion and the security together are not enough. A strong file usually trades one against another: more paid-in equity and cleaner security are the arguments that win you smaller, shorter guarantees.
checklist: The stack ranks senior, mezzanine, preferred, common.
Losses run from the bottom; the senior lender is cushioned by everything below it.
Equity must be paid in, rank behind the bank and carry no side deal.
Intercreditor agreements govern priority and enforcement between lenders.
Security includes step-in rights through contract assignments and a share pledge.
Limit guarantees and make them burn off; write down your worst-case exposure.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A mezzanine lender offers to fill your equity gap, and your senior bank says it will allow it only with an intercreditor agreement and a standstill. What does that mean for the mezzanine lender, and how does it change your risk?
selftest.a: It means the mezzanine lender will be paid only after senior debt, and on default must wait for a set standstill period before enforcing, while the senior bank controls the process. For you, it adds a fixed, higher-cost claim above your common equity, increasing leverage: your equity is smaller and is wiped out by a smaller fall in value, and distributions stop sooner if rent falls short.

apply: Without notes, explain aloud in two minutes the difference between security and a guarantee, with one example of each.
